To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) A combination of a bridge and a crostalk can result in a slowdown that is greater than the sum of the slowdown caused by each effect, in isolation; (ii) A combination of bridge and crosstalk can result in a speedup that is greater than sum of the speedup caused by each effect; and (iii) A bridge at a crosstalk site can invalidate a crosstalk test vector.

the presence of a bridge at a site can significantly affect the slow-down/slow-up of a crosstalk fault at a separate site, and a crosstak test vector may be invalidated by the presence of a defect at the crosstak site.

a weak bridge at one site, and crosstalk at another site, can cause slowdown/slow-up whose magnitude can be significantly greater than the sum of the slowdown/slow-up caused by the bridge and the crosstalk in isolation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a test framework that can effectively detect crosstalk and resistive bridge defects in the presence of each other.
the development of a framework for the analysis of crosstalk and bridge defects.
the development of test generation algorithms for crosstalk and bridge defects.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence of weak bridges in the design can significantly affect the crosstalk testing and hence, the crosstalk test development process.
crosstalk and weak bridge defects are highly coupled and a test for crosstalk must be developed by taking into account the presence of weak bridges and vice versa.
a test vector for crosstalk is not valid in the presence of a bridge defect, and vice versa.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the framework proposed in this thesis can be used as an effective guideline in the design of test vectors and in the selection of test sites for crosstalk.

the proposed approach can be used to identify the most critical crosstalk vectors and the most critical crossovers for a particular design, and then to develop a set of test vectors to detect these crosstalks and weak bridges.
the presence of a bridge at a site in its fan-out (or vice-versa) can significantly impact crosstalk detection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is imperative to consider the effects of bridges and crosstalking in conjunction with one another, in order to avoid false positives and false negatives during test development.
a comprehensive test solution for crosstalk needs to take into account the presence of weak bridges in the design.
the presence of weak defects can have a significant impact on the test generation process for crosstalk and that the test vectors generated for one defect can be invalid for the other.
